reading.rtitle: Why the Second Generation Is the Hard One
paras: Family firms make up about two thirds of all companies in the world, and the statistic that follows it is quoted almost as often: roughly a third survive into the second generation, and about one in ten reaches the third. The usual explanation is money, and the usual explanation is wrong. Firms that fail at the handover are rarely the ones that were losing money at the time. They are the ones that had never separated two things which look identical from the inside: owning a company, and being allowed to decide what it does.

The person who takes over almost always inherits the technical job as well. You become the head of the firm on a Monday and you are still the engineer, the baker, or the one who knows the machines, because that is what you were on the Friday. Nobody hands you the other half, and there is no obvious moment to ask for it. Meanwhile the founder's legacy is doing quiet damage. The prices are still set the way he set them, the client list is still the one he built, and the blind spot is not that the successor cannot see the problem: it is that the problem has never looked like one.

Advisers who work with these companies tend to give the same two pieces of advice, and neither is glamorous. Write the governance down while it is still boring, because it will not be boring later. And bring somebody in from outside the family before you need to. The firms that have weathered three downturns and reached a third generation almost all did the second thing early, and afterwards they describe it in the same words: they do not regret hiring the outsider, they regret the years they spent deciding to.

listenings.text: My grandmother founded this company in 1961, in a building we still use, and I will tell you what has not changed since: the building, and the recipe. Everything else has. I am the third generation, which sounds impressive until you find out how few of us there are. The year I would rather not talk about is 2014. My father got sick very suddenly and there was no succession plan, not one page, and for a while three different people in the family believed they were in charge. Nobody was lying. Nobody had ever written it down. That year cost us eighteen months and the biggest client we had. So what I have done since is unglamorous. I have written everything down, and I have brought in two people from outside the family, which my grandmother would have found insulting and which has saved us twice. My advice, if you want it, is to have the conversation while it is still boring. It is never boring later.

I go into a lot of family companies, and I ask the same question in the first meeting: who decides? It sounds rude. It is the most useful ninety seconds of the year. If two people answer at the same time and give different names, I already know where that year is going to go. The blind spot is almost always the same one. Owners confuse ownership with authority, and those are not the same thing at all. It is not that they disagree about the decision. It is that nobody has ever written down who gets to make it, and an argument about who decides costs more than any bad decision I have ever seen taken. On hiring, the companies that have survived into a third generation almost all brought somebody in from outside early, before they needed to. And afterwards they say the same thing. They do not regret hiring that person. They regret the years they spent deciding to.
